task_row_model.query: When should I use a Python generator expression instead of a list comprehension, and how do they differ in memory usage and evaluation timing?

documents.content: List comprehensions produce a complete list immediately by evaluating the expression for every item in the input sequence. Because they allocate a Python list containing all results, memory usage grows with the number of produced elements. Use list comprehensions when the dataset is small or when you need random access, indexing, or multiple passes over the results. They are also convenient when you intend to modify or inspect elements repeatedly. For very large inputs, creating a full list can cause high memory consumption and slower startup time due to allocating all elements up front.

documents.content: To create an isolated Python environment for a project, use the built-in venv module: python -m venv env. Activate the environment (source env/bin/activate on Unix or env\Scripts\activate on Windows) before installing packages with pip so dependencies stay local. Virtual environments prevent version conflicts between projects and let you pin package versions in requirements.txt. For reproducibility, record exact package versions and consider using pip-tools or poetry. Note that virtual environments affect installed packages, not Python language constructs like comprehensions or iterators.

documents.content: Prefer a generator expression when you want lazy evaluation and minimal memory overhead. Generator expressions produce items on demand and do not build a full list, so they are ideal for processing large or streaming datasets, piping into functions like sum(), any(), or a for loop. List comprehensions evaluate immediately and store all results in memory, which is useful when you need indexing, slicing, or multiple passes. Generators are single-use (they get exhausted), so convert to list() if you must iterate multiple times. Syntax differs: list uses brackets [..], generator uses parentheses (..).

documents.content: Generator expressions create values on the fly and are evaluated lazily as you iterate. They are written like comprehensions but with parentheses: (x*x for x in iterable). Because they yield items one at a time, they can reduce peak memory usage for large sequences and integrate well with functions that consume iterables. A generator will be exhausted after iteration, so attempting to iterate it again yields nothing unless you recreate it. They are also compatible with itertools utilities for composing pipelines without allocating intermediate lists.

documents.content: Python’s list.sort() method sorts a list in place and returns None, modifying the original object; sorted() returns a new sorted list from any iterable. Both accept key and reverse parameters, and Python uses a stable Timsort algorithm under the hood. Use sort() when you want to reorder an existing list without allocating a new one, and use sorted() when you need to keep the original order or need a sorted result from a non-list iterable. Sorting is a different concern than how you generate sequences and does not directly address lazy evaluation.
